Did you like the first Tomb Raider reboot? You'll like this.

Debating which one to get? Get the first reboot first, then get this.

This Tomb Raider game is great - it is gorgeous, it does everything the first game did, and more.

To compare the two:
Rise of has way fewer (almost no) quicktime events.
Rise of is easier. You have all the weapons and abilities of the earlier games, but now you can "craft" grenades and powerful hollow point or explosive ammo on the fly. Armored enemies don't matter.
Rise of doesn't have the same character development. Lara is pretty much a badass at the beginning, and a badass at the end. (Vs the original reboot, where she starts as a whimp and learns to be tough).
If you are debating a cheap version vs a digital deluxe or something...
Baba Yaga: The best type of DLC - adds an additional level to explore, gives you a comical outfit, and unique weapon. The weapon is not overly super powered (but Rise of is a pretty easy game), but it is fun.
Blood Ties: It's pretty much "Gone Home," with Lara Croft. You explore her mansion, looking for a information to keep her evil uncle from evicting her. There's a lot of exploring, and reading, and audio logs, but no combat. I guess its ok if you are into lore.
Endurance Mode: I didn't try, because I hate that stuff. I gather it is some sort of Minecraft where you gather resources and see how long you can live.
Extra outfits/weapons: I found "Rise of..." to be a pretty easy game, so using pay-to-win weapons and outfits felt extra cheaty to me, and I didn't use them.
Remanant Resistance: Adds some fetch quests that you can do midway through the game. They're not bad, but again, since the game is pretty easy, getting more powerful rewards felt cheaty to me.
Cards nonsense: The game lets your replay levels for points. You can use "cards" to give yourself buffs, debuffs, or cosmetics that change your points for the level. I guess its ok, if you are looking to play this games for hundreds of hours, but otherwise they are skippable.

Writing a review in 2025 for a game that was released in 2016 and that I have played and completed at least 5+ times feels quite strange. Nevertheless, I don't want to pass by without saying a few words about this game. Instead of writing a typical review, I'm gonna share my thoughts as someone who has almost completely finished, even exhausted, the game's content.

In the journey that began with the renewed Lara, I believe Rise of the Tomb Raider is the only game that successfully accomplished its mission. Unlike the absurdity of the first game's promised "birth of a survivor" story in the trilogy, this time Rise of the Tomb Raider is a game that successfully hits its target. I used these expressions cuz Lara turns into almost a terminator just a few hours into the first game, nvm though I still consider that game successful for its time but the 2016 Tomb Raider rly shows us the Lara the developers aimed to portray.

Yes, regardless of which difficulty setting u play on, we're still facing a game that doesn't challenge us too much but at least this time, we can clearly see that Lara has shed her naivetythrough her dialogues, reactions to events and inner thoughts. Lara is now more pragmatic (compared to the previous game) and more resilient against challenges. Based on this analysis, I'd say that the most beautiful and character fitting Lara Croft modeling in the new trilogy is also in this game. However, I must mention a deficiency I noticed without giving a negative mark here. Lara, who feels more lively in response to the commands we give in the third game, appears more pale in this game. I think this might be due to the release year difference between the two games.

While my sentences comparing the games among themselves r still fresh, let me immediately say that compared to the boring environmental design of the previous game, this game is really much more successful. 

Not because of the graphic and texture differences between them, but in terms of designing maps, locations and environments, this game is significantly superior. And even raising my claim a notch higher, I must say that I think it's even better than the 3rd game in the series.

The Soviet sections in this game often reminded me of the maps with rusty metal war camps in the first game, and I have to admit that sometimes I found these sections a bit tedious but apart from this, especially in the geothermal valley region and the remaining other areas, I really enjoyed playing every time.

However, I can't say the same praise about the AI of the enemies in the game. Especially on the hardest settings, I saw that the enemy AI went quite off track. Right here, I also want to point out another mechanic I disliked: the mechanism of a special bow we gained after playing the game's DLC and the poisonous arrow that we could use specifically for it is also another thing that looks nice on paper but fails in implementation. Speaking of DLC, it came to my mind that we can only reach a collectible item on the DLC map with an apparatus we gained near the end of the game.

In addition to these, another negative point I want to mention is the sound errors, especially when we start sliding from one place to another on wires, u can notice that the same sound goes into a loop. If u're someone who pays attention to details like me, this can get a bit annoying. I must also say that there r audio sync issues in some metal platform areas.

Apart from this, another issue is that normally many games implement a mechanic known as Coyote Time, which slightly forgives late inputs to create a smoother experience for the player. The same mechanics r certainly available in this game as well but on the contrary, in the surfaces where Lara climbs with her axe, I witnessed many situations where the character dies or cannot complete the movement even in correctly performed actions. This was quite frustrating at times.

Another system that I believe needs to be developed a bit better is the features we unlock from the skill tree with experience points. Since I've completed the game many times, acknowledging that I might be tolerating some of these with my own play style, I must also add the following: to unlock some skills, u need to have another skill that is conditioned as a prerequisite. And these things r so unrelated and non complementary to each other that when finally gain that skill, it's no longer useful to use it cuz u've already progresed in different ways.

Another weak point in the game would be that the game is overly generous with ammo n resources, even on the hardest difficulty. So I never once felt pressured by resource management. 

And the items we can purchase from the merchant with ancient coins are somewhat attractive but the rewards from NPC missions are not. Always earning the same type of (bow) reward loses its appeal after a point. And I must also say that most of these missions are content padding. My main motivation for completing them was the related Steam achievement, not the rewards. Overall, these side missions feel reminiscent of the overly forced and unnecessary content often found in Ubisoft titles.

As for the characters beyond Lara, I must say that the side characters and especially Jonah were written very superficially. Especially the characters in the position of the game's main villains r processed in such a clichéd way...  Also, considering the weight of the story, the dialogues of friendly NPCs remain so empty and meaningless that they are disappointing in themselves, although they're not as nauseating as the dice losing NPC child incident in the next game in the series.

When it comes to graphics, considering the year it was released and the available technology at that time, nothing negative comes to my mind. Although distant renders look a bit bland and pale, when graphics r considered as a whole this is rly one of the things this game is successful at. 

On the other hand, I'd have liked to hear more memorable music in such a game but unfortunately I think the soundtracks quite ordinary in this regard. But there is one track I absolutely adore: I Shall Rise, composed n performed by Karen O. for this game. Its rly among my favorites in game music.

Well, I don't want to drag on at length about a game that most of the community already has a good or bad opinion about. I feel I’ve already said quite a lot about it. In the new generation Tomb Raider trilogy, this is definitely the most successful game in my opinion. So if u’ve read this far thank u for your time.

[h1]Rise of the Tomb Raider V Tomb Raider[/h1]

Crystal Dynamics are the kind of developers to look up too. I absolutely loved the first Tomb Raider. The mechanics were great from the start. The visuals are just incredible. They nailed the sound effects and the story keeps you on edge throughout. The only thing was the multiplayer was pretty boring and there wasn't much to do besides side-quests and getting 100% completion on singleplayer once the story was completed.

Rise of the Tomb Raider is doing what all the successful sequels in the naughties did: Kept the mechanics very familiar if not the same to the last game, but added a few new mechanics on (such as the grappling hook). This is great as you don't have to get used to new controls and too many new items and you get the same nice feeling as the last game.

What I am saying is when CD were developing ROTTR they took into account both the pros AND cons of the game. So in Rise of the Tomb Raider, you have yet another fantastic, immersive story and beautiful visuals. But they have also added lots of new content to play afterwards. They have a small DLC story where you get to look into Lara's past (and her parent's past) if that's what you're interested in. Some fun game modes to try along with the ability to add cards to change the flow of that mode (like the big-head enemies).

The Good:

* Amazing graphics upgrade compared to the previous iteration (Tomb Raider 2013) - 
  though at a heavy performance cost
* (Somewhat) Intriguing story
* Upgraded combat mechanics
* Upgraded stealth and stealth kill mechanics
* Top-notch cast and acting
* Good DLC
* Croft Manor is back! Although no locking the butler in the fridge this time :( :D

The Bad:

* Swimming is fairly non-interactive (no hunting for underwater items, no underwater fights)
* Saving makes even less sense than before with "sitting by the fire at base camp"
  between fights in obvious war zones. It just ruins the whole illusion of being in the game.
  One minute you're fighting for your life, the next you're sitting at a camp fire while a few 
  yards away another big fight awaits...
* Weapon upgrading and item purchasing takes some serious effort - 
  to the point of being annoying

The Ugly:

* Tedious to get all of the achievements - even more so because many of them 
  require multiplayer / co-op.... so very unwarranted in what is obviously primarily 
  a single player game

Synopsis:

Rise of the Tomb Raider picks up where 2013's Tomb Raider left off with a more experienced Lara Croft - on the way to becoming the superheroine she is meant to be - but not quit there yet. Lara is obsessed with uncovering the mysteries surrounding her father's life's work and untimely demise. Inevitably this causes her to get on the evil organisation Trinity's radar - and then as they say: the game's afoot. Lara finds herself competing with Trinity to find the 'divine source' and the adventure begins.

--- Review ---

Gameplay:

3rd person perspective game with advanced climbing and traversal mechanics as well as an intuitive stealth combat and projectile combat system. Lara's nowhere near the super gymnast she was in the original games - but all the added mountaineering, rock climbing and tree climbing really make up for it.

Combat:

Lara's iconic dual-pistol wielding was largely swapped out for bow and arrow in the previous game - a new tradition continued in this one. Personally I think this was a good move in terms of elegance, realism and an overall expanding of the 'adventurous feeling'. There are many other weapons to choose from as the game progresses of course - but the bow quickly becomes the go-to weapon for killing baddies and hunting - as it is also a mainstay for puzzle solving and traversing all of the hazardous terrain.

Compared to the previous game the stealth mechanics have been greatly upgraded - allowing for a much more enjoyable experience when getting through combat areas. Climb up a tree - look for a couple of baddies grouped together and shoot a poisoned gas arrow in their midst. After that lunge out of the tree and stealth kill the baddie passing by before stealth finishing the next one. Highly enjoyable compared to the heavy reliance on brawling and gun fighting in the previous game. Brawling simply doesn't match Lara's redesign in my opinion. Although this game does still have plenty of brawling moments as well - but much less so.

Last but not least: there's a fair amount of mid-battle explosives crafting in the game which - once mastered - can be quite interesting and fun. Proximity mines out of enemy radios, molotov cocktails out of booze bottles (that are simply everywhere somehow) - and smoke bombs out of empty cans. All of which can be very effective - if used correctly.

Puzzles:

As with all Tomb Raider games - there are plenty of puzzles to solve and challenge tombs to find, each of which will give you special skills and upgrades. Although finding some of them is a bit of a challenge in itself - they honour the Tomb Raider spirit.

Enemies / AI:

The AI varies greatly from zone-to-zone - but I can't explain that without same major spoilers - so I won't :)

Graphics:

Compared to the previous game the graphics have been greatly upgraded; Lara's hair looks more natural than ever, her face more detailed and expressive - and the environments just keep getting better and better. Simply gorgeous.

Performance:

All that upgraded eye candy comes at a heavy cost - while the previous game was humble in its requirements yet still a very very good looking game - this one has almost doubled the system requirements.

Using my main Single Board Computer (sporting a Core m3-7y30 and 8Gb RAM) it will play nice at 1024x768 resolution - which the engine re-scales to a 16:9 perspective anyway which is a very nice feature :)

It is playable on my previous Single Board Computer (sporting a Core m3-6y30 and 4Gb RAM) at 800x600 - but with barely enough frames per second to still be enjoyable.

Anything higher than a CPU with an integrated Intel HD 515 or HD 615 GPU - should do nicely.

Note: Don't let Intel's restarted numbering system fool you though: the 4xx, 5xx, 6xx and Iris versions actually perform a little better than the 4xxx, 5xxx - that you'll find on Desktop CPU's such as (older) i3 and i5 chips.

Despite being a 'mobile' CPU - Core M usually has a GPU that's a little faster than full blown i3 and i5 CPU's from a year before. 

Most reasonable discrete GPU's from AMD and Nvidia should perform a lot better of course - especially in the GTX 1xxx range (or comparable). If you have that - then the game should play very nicely at 1080p or more :)

But as I am a Single Board Computer Gamer - I am happy that all of the new Tomb Raider games are actually playable on Intel HD 615 and above :)

Price:

Well worth the money when it originally came out and even more so now that the price has dropped. Its a great game with hours and hours of gameplay (I clocked 60 on this one) - I definitely recommend it.

Conclusion:

Even though the shock and awe that the first game delivered has faded - this game did not disappoint. Its upgraded in every way - stunning even by the standards of 2019 - and will give you hours and hours of fun - while seeing Lara come yet another few steps closer to the superheroine she will ultimately become.

Score:

88 out of 100.

At long, long last...the Tomb Raider game I always hoped for!

   Yeah, I know that sounds incredibly selfish, and yeah, I know that in the eyes of many that instantly makes me a philistine. Three words to you people: eat a dick. I've been patient. I've been a good boy. I'm in my early forties, and finally, the enormous potential which I felt this character and franchise always showed has been fulfilled.

   Allow me to qualify this a little. Firstly, as much as I loved the very first Tomb Raider way back in the day, and at least liked some of the ones after that, they were always a bit "hard" for me, especially on a puzzle and spacial level. Trying to work out what to do or where to go next was like pulling teeth in those early games, and while I appreciate a lot of people enjoy that level of immersion and challenge, it was always a bit much for moi.

   I did get through the very first Tomb Raider on the Playstation 1 with a bit of persistence and a wee bit of help from my friends - without whom I never would have found the lost valley with the T-Rex in it, so near to the beginning! - but that was the last game of the initial "series" I ever completed. Others were interesting, but just so stoopidly feckin' hard that I eventually gave up. So not quite the series for me.

   Then came the recent reboot, or if you like, first game in this "current" series. While it dumbed things down sufficiently for a spazmo like yours truly, it perhaps OVER-did it, almost entirely replacing puzzles with an excess of combat and "action".  And while I appreciated the shift from almost family-friendly fight scenes to balls-to-the-wall brutality, one couldn't help but feel they'd gone a little TOO far away from the spirit of the original games, not least of all in the fact that there weren't that many actual TOMBS to be RAIDED.

   Enter this second game in the reboot series, and whad'ya know? MAGIC, MOTHER-FUCKERS.

   This is the Lara Croft game I always lusted after: constantly gritty and atmospheric, often spooky and violent, with enough well-designed puzzles to slow me down a tad without ever bringing events to a complete stand-still. Hands-down, this is the best iteration of the Tomb Raider universe for me yet: games, movies, you name it. This is the one.

   It begins with one of the best openings to a game ever - well, okay, two of them (the prologue in the snow AND the first tomb proper, in Syria) - and it remains pretty consistent from there. Even the hunting mechanics which were slightly tiresome in the last installment seem more "necessary" and fully realised this time around, and the crafting system far more rewarding (the skill system is much the same as last time, but certainly nothing to complain about). And the combat, which I couldn't help but feel was a tad unwieldy at times in the prior game, is much smoother this time around; oh, and there's far, far less of them pesky Quick-Time Events, praise the Gods. Improvements aplenty, in other words.

   Sure, there's one or two alterations/additions which are a bit silly - increasing your proficiency in languages just by looking at pretty pictures on the walls, for instance - but nothing which impedes the enjoyment of the experience in any notable way, shape, or form. It's also nicely designed in the way that it caters so well to both linear-lovers like myself and people who like their gaming worlds a little more "open": there's tonnes of side-missions to undertake and extras to explore, and they're varied enough from the path of the main game that even I ended up doing most of them (unlike, say, the Borderlands games, which are like a non-stop barrage of very similar missions in all-too-same-ish scenery, over and over and over again).

   Games don't get much more glorious than this. Recommended to...just about anybody and everybody, really.

[h1]Trinity Enters[/h1]

[b]*minor spoilers ahead in this paragraph*[/b]

The antagonist of the previous episode wasn't exactly convincing or interesting. To raise the bar we now have Trinity; an organisation who the main villains work for. Konstantin and Ana represent a dangerous team and it is interesting to see why they pursue the artefact what Rise of the Tomb Raider is all about. We get to see a lot more of Lara's emotional side, too, with particular emphasis on her relationship with her father. Once more we have many cutscenes as we play through the story; the flashbacks shedding light on some past events (most notably on Ms Croft's childhood) are also regular.

[h1]Rise of The Foundation[/h1]

New game but with the same, reworked engine. Our journey now takes us to Syria (only in the prologue) and to Siberia. The snow-covered areas look beautiful and in general we have a lot of places with gorgeous vistas in the background. Snowstorms and Lara's footsteps in the snow look very realistic; water effects (waterfalls in particular) also stand out and my favourite was the geothermal valley with its gas effect and lush flora. Although the game looks better it is not optimised that well - a little tweaking is required to get the desired 45-60 FPS values. I did some workaround with the textures, to be specific, but some say turning off DX12 can also help. 

[h1]Improved Upon Game Mechanics[/h1]

This is a new, refined Lara who comes prepared for a mission. She does not have a torch but always uses a glowstick to illuminate a cave. Weapon categories are kept but each category has more items. Crafting also returns and we now have more skills to purchase at the almost 50 camp sites we can discover. Lara's outfit can also be changed in camps - it's mainly a cosmetics feature but some costumes give us some advantages.

One thing we'll notice is how big the game became. Some locations are central areas we later on return to as the story progresses. As we unlock new items (such as the wire spool) we can return to previous areas to enter caves or other places we were unable to visit. If you are an achievement hunter you'll regularly visit "old" campsites to look for some collectibles and complete challenges.

One great addition to the game is the ad-hoc weapon crafting option. We can make Molotov cocktails or smoke grenades on-the-fly or even use an enemy's corpse as a trap. The crafting options are area specific and as they make fighting more interesting you may prefer the all-out war method to the stealth mechanics. The latter, of course, also returns and we can once more use the environment to attack enemies from above or even from underwater. There are more tombs, more wild animals and even optional missions to complete for extra reward!

[h1]Survival of The Fittest[/h1]

There are a lot of DLCs available - most of them are just cosmetics (such as the outfits) or simply not long enough to be worth purchasing. There are two I really liked and since they cannot be reviewed separately on the store page I am including them here. One of them is [i]Baba Yaga[/i] which is actually part of the Slavic folklore. Since we visit a Soviet installation during the story adding extra content on a supernatural being was a great idea. It adds a decent number of hours to our walkthrough that can already reach 30-40 hours in case you want to explore and find everything. Baba Yaga has a new outfit and a special bow for us for later usage.

The other one is [i]Endurance mode[/i]. Lara finds herself in the Siberian wilderness and her task is to collect artefacts. As the days past (with visible day-night cycles) Lara gets hungrier and colder. Hunting is a must to find food and lighting a base camp is also a means for survival. Time flies and our enemies change - rabbits and deer will be replaced by lynxes and bears and enemy soldiers get better weapons and armour. It's also nice seeing the two fighting - we can step in once a bear rid the forest of 3-4 enemy combatants.

There are ruins, various shelters and enemy-inhabited camps to explore. Our main goal is to find crypts that are full of traps and artefacts. This mode (similarly to other DLCs) utilises the card system. Cards get dropped as we complete Lara's new journey. These items modify our score at the end of every expedition. They can grant us with an increase or with a decrease. For instance, if we want to start in the wilderness with a fully upgraded pistol 20-30% will be taken off from our score at the end. Making small animals inedible will grant us a 100% extra, though. We can also replace all soldiers with infected Soviet population - a more menacing type of enemy that mainly uses melee. 

Endurance greatly increases the game's longevity and playing it in coop is an option which also means we can say good-bye to the previous episode's multiplayer mode. 

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

RoTT offers a smoother gaming experience. It looks better, it lasts longer and it significantly raises the bar its predecessor already raised to a very high level. It is the epitome of what a sequel should be. A must-play if you liked Lara's previous outing and please do not take the latest movie adaptation into consideration when deciding whether or not to play this one.

This review is based on 100% completion and 63.2 hours of gameplay. 

[h1][b]Recommendation:[/b][/h1]
Would I recommend this game? Absolutely. I admit I’m heavily biased when it comes to anything related to Lara Croft, but even without that bias, this is a well-crafted game with a strong narrative, amazing graphics and solid gameplay, so I would recommend it regardless.

Like other [i]Tomb Raider[/i] games, this one boasts an engaging and well-written narrative that will keep you hooked from start to finish. The superb sound design and audio, paired with stunning graphics, really enhance the overall experience and work to complement each other in such an amazing way.

The gameplay is familiar if you’ve played other entries in the series. It feels intuitive and works well, with everything complementing each other smoothly. The puzzle-solving elements are not too difficult, and some puzzles are quite unique and enjoyable. The gunplay is decent, although it can feel a bit off on a controller due to the strength of the aim assist and the speed of the reticle movement. However, this can be adjusted and tweaked slightly in the settings, and you’ll get used to it over time.

The DLCs, such as [i]Baba Yaga[/i] and [i]Blood Ties[/i], offer interesting additions to the game's narrative and are fun to play through. While the other DLCs, like [i]Endurance Mode[/i] and [i]Cold Darkness[/i], didn’t add much beyond achievements, they weren’t bad either.

Unfortunately, like other [i]Tomb Raider[/i] games, this one includes challenge modes. I’m not a fan of challenge modes in any game, and as you would expect this features your typical score and time challenges. If you enjoy that sort of thing, there’s plenty here for you to get into.

For issues with the game, I had quite a few crashes, mainly during expeditions. A big problem was that all my screens would go black, and then my GPU would throttle to the max. I was unable to diagnose the problem, so I’m not sure of a specific fix for it—it was basically a 60/40 chance of crashing when it happened. [i](Again, this was only during Expeditions for me)[/i]

Also, the game has an issue with the UI when using a controller—it can be a bit hit or miss, especially when trying to select cards and other items before a score attack or endurance run. So, just keep in mind that sometimes it’s best to use your keyboard and mouse in the menus, as it may throw you straight into the game when you’re trying to select a card to use.

One thing to note: if you’re planning to play Endurance Mode in co-op, you might need to roll back the game to version 811.3 [i](beta)[/i] to connect properly with another player. We had connection issues and found this solution online, so it might help if you run into the same problem.

Overall, this is a fantastic game with an amazing story and solid gameplay to back it up. If you take your time and play through thoroughly, you can easily invest many hours into it. The base price is reasonable for the amount of content you get, but since it’s an older game that frequently goes on sale, I’d recommend waiting for a discount if you can. However, if you’re eager to jump in, the base price is fair.

[h1][b]Achievements:[/b][/h1]

[b][i]DLC is required for 100%, and there are also co-op achievements that will require one other player. Be mindful of a few missable achievements as well.[/i][/b]

This game has a large number of achievements spread across the campaign, challenge modes, and DLCs. For my playthrough, I followed an excellent guide on TrueAchievements by Tranierx, which has detailed descriptions, pictures and videos to help with everything you need. The guide is well-organised, making it easy to find specific sections, such as the DLC content. You can view the guide [b][url= https://www.trueachievements.com/game/Rise-of-the-Tomb-Raider/walkthrough] here. [/url][/b]

As for the achievements themselves, thanks to the guide, they are relatively easy, though some are missable. I didn’t encounter any major issues with achievements during my playthrough. However, for the co-op achievements, as mentioned earlier, we had to roll back the game to version 811.3 to play together, so keep that in mind.

The main hurdle you’ll face is the score attack achievements tied to the challenge modes. There are a lot of them, and if you’re not a fan of challenge modes like me, they will be tough to get through. They’re the reason I took such a long break between starting and finishing the game. These achievements will take some time, so it’s best to chip away at them gradually and take breaks when needed.

Overall, while the achievements might seem daunting, but thanks to the well-crafted guide by Tranierx, the journey is and was enjoyable—aside from the challenge mode achievements, of course!

[b]Some games are fun. Some games are cinematic. And then there are games like Rise of the Tomb Raider, the rare breed that make you feel like you are the protagonist. That every cliff you climb, every relic you discover, every pulse-pounding escape sequence is your story. And if I’m being honest… I didn’t just play this game. I lived it.[/b]

[h1]Lara Croft: The Queen of Adventure[/h1]
[b]Let me be absolutely clear, Lara Croft isn’t just another video game character to me. She’s the gold standard of female protagonists. Intelligent, brave, ruthless when necessary, yet deeply human. She doesn’t just dual-wield pistols, she dual-wields inspiration and chaos. If Lara Croft walked into my life for real, I’d probably faint… then immediately ask her to teach me how to climb a deadly mountain with just a pickaxe and pure stubbornness.
And Rise of the Tomb Raider is one of her finest portrayals. This game dives deep into Lara’s psyche, her motivations, her obsessions, her vulnerabilities. It’s not just about raiding tombs; it’s about understanding the kind of person who chooses to walk into danger willingly.[/b]

[h1]Gameplay & Exploration – Archaeology with Adrenaline[/h1]
[b]The world is big, beautiful, and begging to be explored. Snowy Siberian peaks, forgotten crypts, lush ruins, all filled with puzzles that make you feel clever without requiring a degree from Hogwarts. Hunting animals, crafting gear, sneaking through enemy camps like a silent British ninja, there’s always something satisfying to do.
And don’t even get me started on the side content. Croft Manor, Lara’s Nightmare, time trials, collectibles… Yes, I became that person who checked every cave, every crack in every wall. If Lara can loot it, I will loot it.[/b]

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*]Incredible world design and exploration
[*]Deep, emotional look at Lara’s character
[*]Satisfying combat and stealth mechanics
[*]Gorgeous visuals that still hold up
[*]Tons of extra content and replayability
[/list]
[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list]
[*]The price still clings to life like an enemy soldier refusing to go down
[*]Lara makes me feel deeply unaccomplished as a human being
[/list]
[h1]Verdict[/h1]
[b]With nearly 160 hours in the game, I can confidently say: Rise of the Tomb Raider isn’t just an adventure, it’s a pilgrimage. A journey with one of gaming’s most iconic heroines at her absolute best.
If you’ve ever dreamed of being an explorer, if ancient myths fascinate you, or if you simply love strong characters with even stronger determination, play this. Treasure it. Become one with the pickaxe. Highly Recommended. Lara Croft forever.[/b]

While I really liked Tomb Raider (2013), I can't say the same about this game, unfortunately. It's not that this is a bad game per se, but it doesn't have the same magic as the 2013 installment. The main reason for this is the setting and storyline; Tomb Raider felt like a very self-contained game, telling a very focused story – Lara's first-ever adventure, being stranded on a mysterious island and not only trying to survive (mostly by herself) but also uncovering the supernatural secret the island holds. This game, on the other hand, essentially follows Lara trying to find a mystic artifact, racing Trinity on who finds it first. While this could be interesting in theory, it lacks any sort of focus. Lara is no longer fighting by herself for survival but is constantly around other characters who are a huge focus of the story, yet completely uninteresting. At no point did I care about them or what happens to them – this alone is obviously a major problem if the game focuses on their backstory as much as it does.

I can't really fault the gameplay, as it's essentially the same as in the previous game and works really well for the most part. However, I do have a problem with the level design; maybe my memory is a bit cloudy, but I don't remember the previous game being as open and having this many collectibles. This leads to a lot of areas being enormously huge to make room for said collectibles, but if you're like me and not interested in those, it also leads to a ton of running around on flat terrain to progress the story. For me, this ruins the game's pacing quite a bit, which just feels very slow compared to the previous one.

On a more positive note, the graphics are great. Lighting, vegetation, animations, and reflections all look fantastic. Especially the facial animation received a huge upgrade (although I prefer Lara's design in the previous game, as it had a lot more personality).

Overall, this game simply failed to engage me in the same way the previous one did. If you're looking for a focused, self-contained, and (most importantly) fun game to play, get the previous installment instead.

[h2][b]The Best Lara Croft Has Ever Been[/b][/h2]

First things first, thank God they finally introduced [b]sprinting[/b] in this game. After playing Tomb Raider, it’s a small change that makes a surprisingly big difference.

This sequel, which many consider the strongest entry in the reboot trilogy, builds directly on the foundation laid by the previous game. It delivers a familiar but refined experience that leans heavily into exploration, cinematic storytelling, and classic tomb-raiding adventure.

The story takes place one year after the events of the previous game and once again puts you in the boots of Lara Croft as she searches for the legendary lost city of [b]Kitezh[/b]. Most of the adventure unfolds in the frozen wilderness of Siberia, where snowy mountains, abandoned installations, and hidden tombs create a fitting backdrop for the journey.

Gameplay will feel very familiar to fans of the first game. It blends third-person action with stealth combat, puzzle solving, exploration, and resource gathering. The core systems haven’t changed dramatically, but they’ve been polished enough that the experience rarely feels outdated.

Exploring optional tombs and discovering hidden areas is easily one of the highlights. If you enjoy environmental puzzles and uncovering hidden treasures, the game delivers plenty of satisfying moments.

Progression comes through crafting, gear upgrades, and a skill system divided into three categories: Brawler, Hunter, and Survivor. These allow you to shape Lara’s abilities around your playstyle without forcing you to stress too much about optimization, since the overall difficulty remains fairly approachable.

Visually, the game has aged quite well. While many environments are dominated by snowy landscapes, the atmospheric lighting, weather effects, and environmental detail still hold up nicely today. Another great touch is the voice-acted collectibles and the language proficiency system, where translating monoliths and ancient documents reveals hidden secrets scattered across the map.

The gameplay itself is fairly straightforward, and like many story-driven adventure games, it’s the narrative that keeps pushing you forward. The story maintains a steady sense of momentum, even if there are a few slower moments along the way.

Overall, Rise of the Tomb Raider delivers exactly what fans want from a modern Tomb Raider experience. If you enjoyed the 2013 reboot or like cinematic action-adventure games similar to Uncharted, there’s a very good chance you’ll enjoy this one as well.

It may not reinvent the formula, but it’s a polished, satisfying adventure that’s absolutely worth picking up, especially if you can grab it on sale.

I can’t believe this game is almost a decade old. It’s absolutely stunning — visually and mechanically — as if it was released this year.  

I jumped into [i]Rise of the Tomb Raider[/i] right after finishing the previous game, and the transition felt seamless. The gear remained mostly the same, with some upgrades. Here, Lara Croft is already an experienced adventurer, so most equipment is available from the start. With the updated graphics, it really felt like a better, stronger version of 2013’s TR Lara.  

However, rushing into this game immediately after finishing the previous one was a bit of a mistake.  

Don’t get me wrong, I really liked it. It’s visually beautiful, the story is decent, all the parkour/combat/puzzles present and accounted for. But the gameplay stayed essentially the same. I’d highly recommend taking a break between TR games to avoid falling into the [i]“eh, more of the same”[/i] mindset.  

This game is about twice as big as its predecessor. More locations, more activities, more tombs, more enemies — literally more of everything. If you’re a completionist, it can get overwhelming fast when trying to explore every nook and cranny.  

[h3]Completionist Complain Corner[/h3]

For me personally, there’s [b]way[/b] too much additional content. You’ve got the main story, main story “chapter” replays, co-op levels, solo and co-op challenges, one story DLC, and a few DLC modes (which are kinda separate replayable “dungeon maps”). While this certainly adds replayability, most of it felt uninteresting or grindy to me. In my opinion, the main story, "Baba Yaga", and "Blood Ties" offer the best experience and are more than enough.  

I also wasn’t a fan of the updated weapon upgrade system. Instead of just one gun or one bow, you now have 3–6 options for each. If you fully upgrade one rifle, you can’t just switch to another without starting the upgrade process from scratch.
To be fair, on normal difficulty, you can ignore upgrades entirely and use any weapon at any time.  

The map is packed with activities, giving me strong Assassin’s Creed vibes, with tons of collectibles that can keep you playing for dozens of hours.  

[h3]Conclusion[/h3]

[i]Rise of the Tomb Raider[/i] is a fantastic game. The fact that you can get it for as little as $5 is almost ridiculous. Definitely grab it if you see it on sale and save it for when you’re in the mood for an adventure!  

But give yourself some time after playing the previous TR game — you’ll appreciate the sequel much more without the risk of burnout.

[b][u]The Basics:[/u][/b]
Rise of the Tomb Raider (RoTR) is an action-adventure game starring one of gaming’s most enduring characters, Lara Croft. In her latest adventure, Lara has to stop a secret society from getting their hands on an ancient relic of enormous power. 

[b][u]Gameplay:[/u][/b]

(I played the game on Survivor, the second hardest difficulty)

RoTR’s gameplay consists of combat encounters and exploration. In combat, Lara is supposedly free to deal with her enemies as she sees fit. So, you can gun down everyone in sight like Rambo, or distract and stealth kill enemies like you’re the Predator. Sounds good, right? Except, no, at many points in the story, the game forces you to fight a bunch of enemies head on. Because I guess the developers thought that stealthing around is for cowards. 

In between the story bits, you’ll be exploring the world, looking for resources and collectibles to build upgrades for your equipment and getting experience points to level up. You can also complete some side quests for additional rewards. The problem is that the game only has two segments which are open ended enough to explore at your own pace. Most of the segments in the game are corridors that you are supposed to pass through while you’re playing the story. And the kicker? The two open parts of the world can be completed in 2-3 hours with the right gear. The whole thing feels like some Ubisoft open world game, with the added caveat of throwing in a few “chest high walls” that you can’t get through unless you play through the story and get the tools needed to pass.

The DLCs have some extra modes, like survival and time attack, which can extend the replay value of the game. I’d suggest anyone looking to buy the game gets those, since the base game is severely lacking in the gameplay. Its not a good thing when I can get the game to 85% completion in 24 hours on the second hardest difficulty level.

[u][b]Graphics and sound: [/b][/u]
The game world is pretty well designed and it looks great on higher settings. You can even see stuff like Lara leaving behind tracks in the think snow as she passes through. The sound design is generally good, although you will often hear the enemies repeating the same 5-6 lines, which gets ridiculous after the 5th time you hear a late game enemy mention that this is their first time working for the bad guys. 

[b][u]The Problems: [/u][/b]
The biggest problems with RoTR are its storyline & characters and its overall lack of a distinguishing feature. 

The game’s plot supposedly explores Lara’s relation with her late father and her attempts to vindicate his lifelong research. However, right in the game’s prologue, Lara sees the lost city she was looking for. Since this means that Lara could just take a picture and head back home, the game immediately introduces a whole “almighty secret society” angle to give her a motivation to get through the rest of the plot. To cover up how hasty this was, the devs included a few throwaway lines in the enemy chatter indicating that the events of Tomb Raider 2013 were orchestrated by the same group. 

None of this would be too bad, if the game treated the plot like a campy B-movie plot. But the writing and dialogue makes it so that everything is super serious. Most of the voice actors try their best to pull this off, with varying levels of success. However, the worst at this is our protagonist Lara Croft. Camilla Luddington, Lara’s VA in the game, hasn’t improved her performance at all since Tomb Raider 2013. As a result, every time Lara says she’s “got to” do something, the only one she manages to convince is herself. 

Another big problem with RoTR is that it has very little to stand out from other action-adventure games like Far Cry or Assassin’s Creed. The whole tomb raiding thing (you know, the thing Lara and this whole remake trilogy is known for?) is pretty much relegated to optional side activities. This is a game that threw everything at the wall to see what would stick, and as a result became something without an identity of its own. 

[b][u]Final word:[/u][/b]
Rise of the Tomb Raider is a functional, if unambitious game that will tide you over if you’re looking for a game that doesn’t do much to stand out from the crowd of better action-adventure games. Its no wonder that the game has been surpassed on almost all aspects by games like Far Cry, Assassin’s Creed and Horizon Zero Dawn since its release. It might not blow you away with its amazing unique gameplay or moving story, but it will tide you over if you’re just hungry for some cheap action.

Rise of The Tomb Raider by Crystal Dynamics
Score 9 / 10 (Solid) 

Great news for Lara fans; the PC version of “Rise of the Tomb Raider” delivers a grandiose noggin scratching ancient history conspiracy theory driven plot pitting the multi-generational Croftian zealotry for ‘divine artifacts’  versus the archetypal villains with too much money, power, and religiosity; ‘follie-a-trois’ n’est-ce pas? More importantly, does this game have puzzles?

Present and expected are the improbably improbable puzzles ubiquitous to the Lara universe; I ‘pray’ for these contraptions with secrets hidden beneath massive moveable walls and oversized cogs each controlled through a series of timed switches powered by gravity and water. A little bit of patience always yields a Codex with life changing knowledge (nudge-nudge wink-wink).  Inexplicably these puzzles seem to have been relegated to the “optional side missions”, a direct in-game quote. These are the classic Tomb Raider pieces that I love and I completed them as soon as possible; they always yielded extra XP, gold coins and skills; I wish these puzzling sections had been way longer. What then is ‘central’ to this digital archeological hunt? Read on….

The main plot unfolds wrapped as a “third person shooter”. Feeling a bit shaky are you? Yep, the spelunking has really taken a back seat to the shooter gameplay. There should have been far more dialogue options for negotiations, skillful stealth mode with zero death, and more creative gameplay in the central campaign.  Has Crystal Dynamics made a choice or a mistake? Don’t get me wrong, I love shooters but not this one. Combat with guns in tight spaces and an over the shoulder camera leads to a poor combat experience. Would you like a game with great combat, weapons and well designed arenas? Try Unreal Tournament 3 Black edition instead. Consequently, I found myself  avoiding all main story paths as long as possible because they were so combat unpleasant, and eventually I set the game to the easiest setting to make these encounters as short as possible. What else made the campaign a grind? The controls are ‘tuned’ for parkour platforming; mid combat my character kept putting away the gun and jumping into water or grabbing a ledge; who wants fudge? The default graphics settings use over-the-top screen effects making it uncomfortable: ‘water splashes on the lens’, ‘depth of field’, and others, all of them summing to a ‘digital finger in the eye’. Thank you Crystal Dynamics for letting me turn off all those ‘enhancements’ in the options menu. 

Crafting and skill trees were welcome and enjoyable although heavily dependent on hunting. The upgrade mechanics lead to a veritable slaughter-fest: I must have killed over 700 bunny rabbits, 300 deer, 50 wild boars, 10 grizzly bears, and a partridge in a pear tree. In fact I started farming previous maps for humans because they had the specialized parts. The weapon upgrades yielded for the most part palpable advantages in engagements: Would anyone like an RPG arrow head? Woooooo!  The remaining XP system felt hollow and served to redirect you back to previous maps, that is, if you want to find all coin stashes, hidden provisions, caves and relics. Meh. This is just a poor substitute for replayability.

Crystal Dynamics have done superbly well with the extra game modes. I was particularly impressed with “Endurance” mode placing Lara in the Siberian wilderness to see how many days you can survive; requirements to eat, stay warm, collect resources, craft, and collect artifacts improve your chance of survival and reward the players having skill. Many players will enjoy “Score Attack” mode, an arcade version of the campaign. “Replay” game mode allows you to compare yourself to your Steam buddies through point accumulation. 

What else should you look forward too?
A visually stunning and sprawling game world. check.
Tons of Steam Achievements. check.
One Special achievement for teaching BBQ chicken to fly. Sweet!
Puzzle deaths: 30 times in a row with a game reload. Blame wonky controls. Rage quit. double check.
‘Collision detection’ that doesn’t know ‘collision’ from a ‘hole in the wall’. triple check.
Excessive grunts, breathing, and expletives in that sublime British accent. Yeah.

Buy this game; all Tomb Raider fans will find something they were looking for and ‘more’. Thumbs up.

[h1]Intro:[/h1]

Three years had passed since the release of 2013's reboot of the TR franchise - a great example of how reboots should actually be done. Crystal Dynamics returned in 2016 with a sequel to the reboot, this time for the PC platform. With the focus on survival like in the previous game, the sequel provides more combat this time around which may or may not stray some fans away.

The game is set in Siberia as Lara searches for city of Kitezh, trying 'to decipher' her father's research work. Although, as expected, she is not the only person on this crazy journey. Trinity, a paramilitary organization has their intentions to get to the city's promise of immortality. As Lara is what stands in front of their goal, she is forced to battle. And so, the Rise of the Tomb Raider's journey begins.


[h1]Story:[/h1]

Trying to decipher her father's research that eventually was the reason for his suicide (watch out for some plot twists down the line), Lara ends up in an expedition in Syria. Her attempt to uncover the tomb of the Prophet of Constantinople is successful, but she ultimately finds the tomb empty. In classic fashion, the main enemy is introduced - Trinity, a paramilitary organization investigating the supernatural.

An assassin infiltrates her home and steals the main link of the story - a book on Russian religious history - which Lara links to Syberia. Not much later, the game follows as you begin your quest to find the truth behind the scenes. Often you will find yourself having to listen to constant tedious and unnecessary references to Lara's father which often reminded me DC and the Batman movies. Lara's moral compass is unstable and could use some work.

WIthout much spoiling, you may or may not notice a plot hole within the story itself. The story will sometimes throw a cliché villain or dialogue here and there. It's certainly nothing special and does not stand out by any means. And while being mediocre at its best, it is there to serve its own purpose and doesn't draw attention much away from the main section that counts - the gameplay.


[h1]Gameplay:[/h1]

Rise of the Tomb Raider's gameplay is very similar to the 2013's reboot and / or the Uncharted series. If you're familiar with how the mechanics function in either of those, it won't be an issue to understand the game's mechanics. While some of the controls have been adjusted and binded differently than in the previous release, the game allows you to change the controls at any given point.

Tons of different puzzles are thrown all around the open world (and are mainly set in the main or secret tombs that you can find). There are cases of predefined scripted events which contain a lot of button smashing, but not as much as in the original. The events' outcome(s), unlike the ones from the Uncharted franchise, are unfortunately predefined just like the course of scenes within an event.

The developers seem to have re-used some recorded dialogue from the 2013 reboot, which is never a great thing. In the meantime, combat has been improved and is, just like the puzzles, forced all around the open world. Luckily, there's a balance between exploration and combat.

On a pretty surprising note, the 2013 reboot's combat, while not the best thing around, was certainly decent at its peak. There's a crafting system that allows you to upgrade the weapons of your choice and improve specific parts, therefore forcing you to change your approach very often, making the gameplay much more fun. Rise of the Tomb Raider takes the concepts and all the positive parts of gameplay from the previous release, expands upon them and when combined with the current engine graphics, provides a totally new feeling.


[h1]Graphics:[/h1]

The "Foundation" engine definitely is one of the top game engines of this generation and if there is one thing that will make me remember this for quite some time, then it's visual presentation of the game. Stunning graphics with really detailed characters, props, weapons and levels provide a lovely feeling.

In one moment you're looking at the beauty of Syria's deserts and in the next you're climbing Syberia's mountains. The game looks simply gorgeous. To fill the feeling with awesomeness are Lara and the side characters. Lara looked really nice in the previous release and here, she is simply beautiful. The details are stunning and the hair effect definitely adds a lot to it. The other characters look really great as well.

Of course, let's not forget the details on all the props and customizable weapons that can be seen when taking a closer look at them. Then, there is the open world itself. Smart level design with a lot of details and colors is something not seen in every game nowadays. Unfortunately, Rise of the Tomb Raider is a beautiful looking game, but it lacks optimization. Frequent frame drops even on the best hardware available right now make the experience less satisfying.

[h1]Verdict:[/h1]

While not everything is positive and there definitely is stuff that can be improved, Rise of the Tomb Raider is a decent game at its worst. Beside a not very well written story, the way scripted events are handled along with optimization issues, the game takes what was great about the 2013 reboot, expands and improves is and provides enough quality for this to be a new release.
 
With quite a few puzzles for some, decent combat for others and stunningly detailed levels and beautiful graphics, Rise of the Tomb Raider is a game worth your attention to say the least.

After playing and enjoying the first game I hoped that Rise of the tomb raider will be an improvement with better gameplay, better story, more locations and tombs. I was wrong, Rise of the tomb raider is worse, they just added more bad things to the game.

Why I don’t like this game? The beginning is great, it makes impression there’s an awesome game awaiting you. But you’re suddenly being thrown into boring open world gameplay. It copies Far cry and Assassin’s creed but is even worse. All you do is collecting garbage. Every 5 meters there’s something to collect, you turn around and there are another 5 things to collect. The locations are empty and boring. The main purpose of those two huge locations is to hide as many collectibles as possible which is a cheap way to prolong the game.
After I finally almost finished the first location and moved with the story I ended up on another location with new garbage to collect. That’s when it clicked for me and I started to hate this game and just finished the story. Instead of giving us 5 or more good and fun different locations like Uncharted we get two shallow locations where we need to find collectibles. No just no.
In short the gameplay is either following the story or running around collecting trash. If you decide to go with the story the game is pretty enjoyable but nothing special. It could be really fun at times.
There are also tombs to explore and raid. They’re fun but most of them are very simple to complete and feel more like just another location to collect worthless crap rather than proper tomb.
The game is not very long but the length is good for an action game, i don't want a 50h action game. You'll be looking into around 15h of gameplay without wasting time on collectibles to complete the game. I've spent 26 hours including DLC, some multiplayer and collecting almost everything in the first location.
There's a multiplayer too in the game. I’ve played it for couple of hours and got bored. You and your friend are being thrown into the wilderness and you must survive together. Collect resources, shoot enemies, avoid traps and survive the night. For those who enjoy multiplayer it could be a positive, but I personally not a fan of that. But keep that in mind.

Graphically the game looks pretty good but I don’t like the sky, same as in first game it looks strange. Other than that game looks great, Lara is well detailed, facial animations are good, cut-scenes are of great quality, environments are breathtaking. Performance on the other hand isn’t good. Whenever I turn on proper AA the framerate drops to 50’s. Absolutely not acceptable forcing people to use FXAA which doesn’t help much. The game came out in 2016 and I have 7700k paired with 1070, I think I shouldn’t have any problems on 1080p.
Voice acting is what you can expect from a triple A game. Sound effects are nice too. Doesn’t matter where you are the sound creates an appropriate atmosphere.

I don’t know how I feel about this game. On one hand if you ignore everything except the story it’s an average game with some really good bits, but if you look at the whole game and how it was designed it’s below average. I can’t recommend it, at least not at the full price. If you can’t live without Lara or actions games buy the GOTY edition on sale. I know there's not a lot of action games on PC so it's understandable. There’s some enjoyable DLC at least.

Regardless of if you’ve played the first game or not, Rise of the Tomb Raider is a journey you should embark on. Few games offer thrills in such a well-crafted, honed package. 
Here is a sprawling, compelling game made with impressive confidence – masterfully paced and expanding on its predecessor without for a moment losing track of its appeal. 
It’s a game that has kept its integrity intact while navigating the weird waters of mass market appeal, and one that retains a real understanding of fundamentally enjoyable mechanics.
There’s simply not a single moment when the game doesn’t feel like it’s not giving its all. Rise of the Tomb Raider truly makes you feel like Lara Croft: a bow-wielding, mountain scaling, bear-slaughtering, cave diving mad lady with more curiosity than can be healthy. And that feeling is just wonderful. Rise of The Tomb Raider is exceptionally easy to recommend.

After the resounding success of the reboot of the Tomb Raider saga , it was clear that Square Enix and Crystal Dynamics would not leave us waiting for another adventure of the most famous tomb raider in video games. In a cloud of controversy over temporary exclusivity, Rise of the Tomb Raider arrives on Microsoft consoles, not as a reissue, but with a title developed for the current generation.

The plot of the Tomb Raider rebootIt was solid and well-written, but it didn't please all the fans, and while it was clear that they had to retell the origins of our protagonist again, it took a more epic touch. As a result, we hoped that in the continuation —and because it was no longer necessary to explain where Lara came from— the story would be deeper. The truth is that once again they leave us waiting for more. The title falls into the cliché of an adventure film: Lara discovers that her late father was behind a mysterious artifact, so she decides to go in search of him to the other side of the world, of course she is not the only one, because a terrible military organization He will do his best to get his hands on the object before Lara. Although the story unfolds apace and never gets boring, The writers managed to evolve into the Lara Croft we met in the previous title. From being a cowardly woman, nervous and afraid of everything, she becomes much more mature, able to face dangers and no longer suffers every time she ends the life of another human being, which gives this Lara a new feeling. From the first moments the developers sought to put her in a position with more power, knowledge, skills and love of mystery; now the protagonist is strong and exploits her abilities to the fullest. Another success is the great voice acting of Camilla Luddington, who brings back the Lara Croft we love: an adventurer who loves danger and mystery.

The tombs are where the developers showed off
The mechanics were kept simple and easy to learn. You have access to weapons such as bows, pistols, shotguns and rifles, each assigned to a button on the GamePad, so just by pressing any direction you can quickly change them. During your adventure you will find new weapons and improvements, in addition to those that you can create with the materials you find. Something very well achieved is the balance between the weapons, because although a shotgun is very powerful, you can add a laser sight to the rifle, although my favorite is the bow. This artifact has secondary options such as poisonous, fire and explosive arrows, which are lethal against large groups of enemies, and because you create them, you almost always have enough.

The fighting style is not perfect, but it is very intuitive, especially with the bow, so it is not long before you begin to execute deadly headshots from several meters away. Lara also fights hand to hand and for that her favorites are the climbing pick and a hunting knife. Although effective, this type of attack is always the last resort, as most enemies have armor and it takes multiple hits to knock them down, which also leaves you at the mercy of gunfire. Of course, being a hunter, Lara gives you the option to avoid combat and choose stealth to stay in the bushes or climb trees while the right time comes to press Y and jump on your enemy to eliminate them in one hit, regardless of their layers and layers of armor. The game lets you choose the type of engagement, but most of the time you choose to shoot, which is more fun thanks to the large number of items you can use to defend yourself. Just imagine there are gas lamps, fuel barrels and more, perfectly positioned to explode with one shot. Something interesting is that the bow and the beak are also necessary to move. The peak is vital for climbing any rocky surface that the game indicates (strangely, you cannot nail it into anything), and as you progress through the story you can use it as a hook to access areas where free climbing is not allowed. The bow is used to launch ropes and join 2 points between which you easily ascend and descend, which is essential to solve puzzles and to move much faster.

In Rise of the Tomb Raider , Lara's hunting sense returns. Pressing the right stick changes the game to shades of gray, but points of interest and interactive objects are highlighted in bright yellow. Almost all the time I used this sense to find hidden objects, know the way to go, and locate enemies — essential if you want to sneak up on you. Although you do not have a limit to the use of this ability, it is much more effective if you remain still, since when you move it vanishes; towards the end of the game you can even see objects through walls and detect animals from a further distance.

Although Lara is now much more skilled, she has a lot to learn, which she achieves by leveling up. The skill tree is much larger as it has more than 50 improvements divided into 3 sections: Combat, Huntress and Survivor, which start out being very different, but as you spend more experience points on each one, they become a general improvement. For example, combat upgrades give more stamina; Jacket allows you to improve your bow handling; and Survivor increases your speed to craft weapons. Leveling up is easy because everything in the world gives you experience: eliminating enemies, collecting plants, finding artifacts, hunting animals, and so on. Of course, not everything is at your fingertips, you need patience if you want to discover the mysteries of all areas. The game could be considered open-world because it is possible to travel the different areas freely, as well as to come and go thanks to fast travel; however, the structure always takes you from point A to B. The developers mask this with the presence of large open areas in which there are hundreds of things to discover. The above is a success, as there are few adventure games — outside of the open world ones — that give a feeling of freedom; in fact, it is increasingly difficult to get us to show interest in a game that does not allow us to go where we want. In this sense, we could say that Rise of the Tomb Raider is not a corridor that you have to go through, but a house with several rooms and a large playground, although you have to use the entrance and exit door.

In terms of settings, this adventure transports you to Siberia, so snow is the general theme. You have around 10 areas to explore, each clearly differentiated from the rest: there will be mountains, glaciers, underwater caves and even greener spaces with waterfalls, and also temples and ruins, as well as abandoned industrial zones. Fast travel is possible thanks to the fact that you find small camps where you can spend your experience points, improve your weapons or change your outfit. Of course, being a game of this magnitude there is a good variety of collectibles in the form of documents and relics that give a little more context to the story, without missing hidden places such as crypts and tombs.

This is a visually stunning story-driven adventure that takes everything that was good about the 2013 game and enhances it. Graphically realistic with a smooth PC-port that has a couple of glitches, but great performance overall. The amount of detail in the background and setting is impressive and immersive whilst seamless integration between cutscenes and action really pulls you into the environment. In short, it looks flippin' awesome.

The controls are smoother than before, with even more climbing, jumping, and in my case, excessive falling. Combat is reactive, and the bow a viable weapon choice - so much better than previously, with added stealth and distractions like a ton of different types of arrows and explosives. The upgrade and crafting system is relatively simple but gives a feeling of growing power as you progress and makes it worth hunting down those extra resources. Puzzles are complicated enough to make me feel smart, whilst not so challenging as to leave me frustrated, and there are an absolute ton of collectibles for the trophy hunters. It starts incredibly linear, but branches out more after the first 60 minutes of gameplay, giving you the option to take on side quests, hunt for collectibles, tackle optional challenges and puzzle tombs, or progress through the main story. Of course, a game like this is always going to be fairly linear overall, but there are enough optional things to make it feel like you have an element of choice and discovery. Oh, and remember those QTE events that were everywhere and annoying as hell? Yeah, they're gone!

The story is decent. It's not breaking any boundaries - but I wouldn't expect it to. It's the origin story of the most famous bad♥♥♥♥♥adventuring lady in the gaming world, who seems destined to save the world and grab some loot along the way. It's what you would expect, a mixed match of legend and history and it works really well. Some of the dialogue and voice actings are top-notch, and some of it leaves a lot to be desired, but even when I'm groaning at the lines or yelling at Lara to stop being so dumb it's still a super fun action-adventure to play, and that's the important bit.

Overall it's a well-crafted balance between story, exploration, brains, and action. For me, it's been a thoroughly enjoyable journey, but hell, if for some reason you hate Lara, you can enjoy the visceral entertainment of even more death scenes, over and over. Enjoy!

[b]I first tried Rise of the Tomb Raider years ago on my old laptop, but it quickly turned into the Crysis of my setup, you know, that legendary game that punishes weak rigs mercilessly. My poor laptop protested harder than Lara climbing a frozen cliff, so I eventually had to quit. Fast forward to now, and with a proper gaming rig in hand, I finally got the chance to see this classic in all its Ultra High glory, and wow, it was like watching Lara Croft come off the screen in full HD sass.

Right from the beginning, the game’s visuals slapped me awake faster than a cold Siberian wind. Snowy peaks, lush forests, ancient ruins, every scene looked like a postcard I’d be proud to wallpaper my desktop with. Seeing Lara in high definition is a joy in itself: every detail from her gear scratches to the frost on her jacket adds layers to her already iconic presence. It’s like watching her level up from pixelated adventurer to movie-ready action hero right in front of your eyes.

Gameplay still holds up beautifully, too. The mix of exploration, stealth, intense gunfights, and clever puzzle moments keeps things moving without ever feeling stale. And even though I’m a seasoned gamer now, those intense climbing sections and timed stealth sneaks still had me gritting my teeth, once or twice I muttered, [i]“Seriously, Lara, grab the edge!”[/i] It’s a perfect blend of cinematic thrills and satisfying mechanics that proves this franchise can deliver on all fronts.

All in all, [i]Rise of the Tomb Raider[/i] clicked with me in a way it never did back in the laptop days, and with good reason. Seeing it run on Ultra High feels like giving Lara the hero’s welcome she deserves. Whether you’re here for jaw-dropping visuals, heart-pounding action, or just to finally see what all the hype was about, this game is absolutely worth your time and your hardware’s love. Now excuse me while I go complain about freezing fields and killer wolves, same old Tomb Raider, just shinier.[/b]

Having just completed Tomb Raider (2013), I was excited to have the opportunity to play Rise of the Tomb Raider (RoTR) and spend additional time with Lara Croft. The second game did not disappoint me and I enjoyed it even more than the original. I played the base game plus two extra segments/DLCs (Baba Yaga, Blood Ties) which added to the overall experience and the back-story of the Croft family. For the most part, game mechanics are the same between games and I was able to jump into RoTR without any learning curve.

I played on 'Adventurer' level (easiest of easy) to reduce the difficulty of combat. This is not the strongest aspect of my personal gaming and I wanted to focus more on narrative and exploration and spend less time dying. The easiest level also removes the requirement that you use crafting to heal. It does not simplify the platforming but my skills increased using the grapple hook and climbing ax to go where no woman had gone before.

Slower (and more fragile) enemies allowed me to use more stealth with the bow and less melee attacks (which are usually fatal for me). Until the final scenes, RoTR seemed to have less 'ambush' scenarios (where dozens of enemies approach you from all sides). It also felt like there was more time to explore locations and look for collectibles without the threat of combat. The challenge tombs seemed a bit less tricky than those in the original game and most did not require perfect timing.

The scenery is lovely, with different archaeological treasures included. The story has depth and I enjoyed getting to know more about Lara and her faithful sidekick, Jonah. The additional characters introduced (Jacob and Sofia) added even more to the story as Lara works with them to defeat Trinity. DLCs that come with the Celebration Edition include extra weapons and outfits which add little to the story but do make Lara look very cool!

I really enjoyed RoTR and am looking forward to the next installment. With the exception of the final boss scene (which was almost impossible for me), I sailed through with minimal frustration and maximum delight as new scenes opened up and I made it through tricky puzzles to move from point-to-point. Luckily, the penalty for dying is non-existent (you just respawn to try again), as I missed jumps or got stomped by enemies often. I freed myself from trying to maximize achievements and, as a result, just had a great time.

Rise of the Tomb Raider is a decent game, but i'm unsure as to whether its better than the 2013 Tomb Raider. They are both similar in a lot more ways than the characters in them. I'll go over the positives of this game first.

The biggest standout in this game for me was definitely the graphics. They are a massive improvement even over the last game and they help to capture a sense of wonder, adventure and beauty that a game like this really benefits from, ranging from vast mountainscapes to shining crypts and tombs. I think the characters were also an improvement from the last game too, Lara feels a lot more confident, independent and she also doesn't spend the entire game making sex noises every 10 seconds like the last game has her doing, the other characters such as Jacob, Ana and Konstantin are also good, with their own personalities, motivations and points of view, the only let down for me was Jonah who felt kinda wasted, especially since he was in the last game.

The other stand out positive for me was the gameplay, the technical aspects of it are basically the same as Tomb Raider 2013 but with some other additions as well, the map and the game itself feels a lot more open, there is more to do including side missions, gathering materials and parts to upgrade weapons and the tombs, where the puzzles are realistic (as in they could actually exist in real life) and require some thought, experimentation and attention to detail, more so than the previous game.

I think the story was a bit of a let down, its not as bad as a lot of other stories i could name but the best words i could use to describe it are "repetitive", "unoriginal" and "hard-work", there is a lot of running around and doing busy-work that isn't necessary and a good portion of the missions have you gathering materials, rescuing someone who got captured in a dumb or unexplained way or just having you spend ages doing something that should take way less time. the plot itself is mostly coherent and definitely fits the whole Tomb Raider theme and vibe, but it basically revolves around "the bad guys are looking for a magical macguffin and the good guys have to stop them", i'm probably being a bit harsh on the story here but it certainly wasn't groundbreaking storytelling either.

Overall, Rise Of The Tomb Raider is a fun and engaging but unrewarding and undemanding action adventure, and anyone who enjoys that kind of game would do well to pick this game up.

Rise of the Tomb Raider improves on its predecessor in almost every way, with better gameplay, better graphics, better sound design, better pacing and most importantly, more actual tombs to exploreI i was dazzled by the size and scope of the island, the fast paced cinematic "escape" sequences, the simple yet captivating shooting mechanics and the boldness of delving so frankly into supernatural territory. Rise of the Tomb Raider just came out a few weeks ago here and I nabbed it as soon as I was able. It delivered everything I expected it would, a decent story with Lara's first encounter with Trinity and the race to find the "Divine source", an object that grants those that gaze upon it immortality before it falls into Trinity's fanatical hands. The combat remains fun, fast paced and somewhat easier with less need to take cover and instead allowing the run and gun approach. The traversal is more detailed this time around, with Lara having more tools at her disposal which unlocks areas previously inaccessible to her, like the Rebreather, Broadhead climbing arrows, and the ability to throw her pickaxe as a grapple hook. The crafting system has been overhauled, with Lara being able to craft bigger ammo and resource storage pouches as well as innumerous upgrades for each variant of pistol, shotgun, machine gun and bow. Most of these upgrades requires special animal hides, which Lara can acquire by finding hidden caches or through good old fashioned hunting. Bears and feral felines make an appearance this time as potential hunts for rare skins, but they won't go down without one hell of a fight... Lara can craft special ammunition on the go and accept side quests from allies who reward her with otherwise unobtainable rewards like new gear or attire. The tombs this time are more numerous and a lot more complicated to solve, at least the first time around. Completing them rewards Lara with unique skills like faster climbing, triple arrow shots and the ability to mine for rare metals required for the best weapon upgrades. There are also crypts in which Lara may find weapon parts and coin caches she can dig up to trade for weapon attachments and unique weapons. Unlike the previous game, it is highly unlikely that you will be able to acquire every skill and upgrade before the end, unless of course you enjoy grinding the same groups of enemies for hours, and so skill and upgrade choices need to be selected more thoughtfully and resources spared for the weapons you enjoy using most. The areas Lara visits are not as numerous as the previous game, but they are unquestionably larger, some maps may take hours and hours to complete while the transition areas usually take about an hour. Not every NPC is hostile towards Lara and there is one particular area that is home to a village filled with friendlies who Lara must help defend against Trinity
