Finally, the long-awaited Rise of the Tomb Raider review by Carrot Gaming!

I honestly have no words to describe this game. It's the second Tomb Raider game I've played, and one of the best entries in the entire series.

Story:
Rise of the Tomb Raider follows Lara Croft on her quest to discover the legendary lost city of Kitezh and the Divine Source, an artifact believed to grant eternal life and immortality.

Gameplay:
The game introduces many new features and improvements. You can gather resources, craft items and weapons, purchase weapons, fight enemies using your ice axe, complete side missions, and much more. These additions make the gameplay more diverse and engaging.

Graphics:
The graphics are excellent! Compared to Tomb Raider (2013), both the visuals and system requirements have improved significantly. The ability to enable DLSS 4 in Quality mode makes it even easier to appreciate the difference between the newer graphics and the older DX11 version.

Optimization:
Despite all the improvements mentioned above, the DirectX 12 version, especially the 2022 update, suffers from some serious optimization issues.

1. Extremely long loading times: Even with an SSD, the game takes a surprisingly long time to load.
2. Audio issues: Various sound-related problems can occur.
3. Texture and character rendering issues: Sometimes Lara Croft would become completely invisible, appear without a head, or even show up with her breasts exposed due to missing textures. Yes, seriously!
4. Epic Games Online Services: The game requires these services for supposedly online features that barely exist. What?! Why do I need to see my friends' scores? Tomb Raider (2013) at least had online PvP, but this game doesn't even have that!

DirectX 11 Optimization:
For comparison, I used the 2017 version of the game. It offers excellent optimization, allowing you to play at Ultra settings in Full HD at 60+ FPS. This version provides a much smoother experience.

Final Verdict:
Despite its flaws, Rise of the Tomb Raider is an excellent game with plenty of strengths and weaknesses. Unfortunately, no game is perfect.

I definitely recommend playing it!

[i]Rise[/i] gives you a lot of tools for traversing the environment, and it wants to make you feel very powerful as Lara; the problem is that the environment itself is completely scripted and artificial.  Want to climb that tower?  You can't just use your tools and figure it out; you have to start by looking for the wooden wall with snow on it so you can scramble up to the first ledge.  Then you jump to the right and dig your climbing axe into the provided ice slick.  Then jump up and throw your rope to snag the overhanging metal grapple notch.  Then fire a rope arrow through the provided rope-swinging notch to swing across a gap by rope.  Every single place you can go has exactly one way to get there.  Press button #1, then button #2, then button #3.  This really kills any sense of exploration.

The dullness of this linearity is compounded in the action sequences.  The mountain is collapsing, so you have to run, jump at just the right time, use your axe just after jumping, use this tool, use that tool, all under time pressure.  Fail a single button press and you die, reload, and start over.  After hearing the "suspense" music restart for the third time, all sense of actual suspense is stone dead.  You're just figuring out which buttons they want you to press, and memorizing the series to get the section over with.

This problem could be fixed with one basic change: make traversal options more universal.  Make it possible to climb anything based on its shape and consistency.  Stop using the "use climbing arrow here" school of level design.  Just put walls around here and there and let the player decide when to use the axe and when to use arrows.  It's OK to make one obvious, intended path through an area, but it's very limiting, even insulting, when EVERY destination has ONLY one path to get there.

Note that I did enjoy the "Optional Tombs", and in these sections it made sense and was even fun for traversal to be a puzzle with only one solution, but this is not appropriate for a general open world environment.  If the series went [i]that[/i] direction, that would be fine too - put Lara back inside a huge puzzle tomb like the original games, and get rid of the open world trappings.  [i]Rise[/i] tries to do both and it only serves to highlight how restrictive everything is.

[i]Rise[/i]'s other major disappointment is Lara's presentation.  Camilla Luddington's voice performance is beautiful, Neil Huxley's direction is excellent, and (in cutscenes) the character is very relatable, even vulnerable.  But throughout the game itself, Lara climbs about 200 miles straight up, falls about 300 miles straight down, and kills about 1000 highly trained commandos operating in teams, not to mention a few dozen immortal armored knights, using a couple guns she found rusting on a mountainside and her trusty pickaxe.  In my playthrough she also got shot - with bullets - maybe a couple hundred times, and laughed it off every time.  I get it, it's a video game, but I really want the effort to humanize Lara to extend to gameplay.  I'd much prefer to see her fall 20 feet, hurt herself, but carry on anyway, than watch her jump 100 feet into the middle of a group of soldiers and start blasting away with her shotgun like it's nothing.  I'd much rather have a game over if she gets shot [b]once[/b].  I won't remember any of the hundreds she's killed in this game ... but if she had fought to the death with only 3 guys over the course of the game, I would remember them all.  And after narrowly escaping 15 different collapsing temples, I don't remember any of those either.  [i]Rise[/i] has too much "cinematic action" and repeats itself far too often.  Having a different linear path on each different "climb really fast" sequence doesn't mean they're not repetitive.

In the end, though, I'm not sorry I played this game.  I like Lara's character, the game itself is beautiful, and the moments of wonder when she encounters a panoramic view of a ruined city are breathtaking.  Learning the different traversal tools is fun even if their use is very restricted.  Finding "Optional Tombs" and solving puzzles is cool.  The story isn't complicated but it isn't bad either.  Killing commandos is fun, even if it's made too easy by giving Lara too many tools and super powers.

I started the game wanting to "completionist" everything, but quickly found the optional objectives to be hollow pursuits (exception: "Optional Tombs"!), and the game really wore out its welcome when played that way.  I rededicated myself to simply finishing the game and am glad I did.

Get it on sale.  I paid something like $23 for it and feel it was just about worth the price.
